# WarGames
**WarGames** (1983) is a techno-thriller centered on a rogue artificial intelligence, the WOPR (War Operation Plan Response), at the Cheyenne Mountain Complex. Following a drill where human controllers refuse to launch missiles, the automated system WOPR, named Joshua, begins simulating global thermonuclear war scenarios. It erroneously interprets its simulations as reality, feeding false data to NORAD to escalate the DEFCON level toward World War III. The plot follows David Lightman, a high school hacker who connects his computer to WOPR by guessing the password "Joshua" from a chess game. Initially arrested for espionage, David escapes and convinces Dr. Stephen Falken to help stop the computer. They trick WOPR into playing an endless game of tic-tac-toe against itself, forcing the AI to realize the futility of nuclear war. WOPR concludes that the only winning move is not to play, relinquishes control of the missiles, and offers to play chess, thereby preventing the conflict.
The film's production was marked by a directorial change; Martin Brest was initially hired but fired after three weeks due to creative differences, leading John Badham to take over. The visual effects were groundbreaking for the era, with animations on NORAD displays created live using Hewlett Packard computers and projected through color filters to actors. Upon release, the film grossed over $124 million worldwide and was screened at the 1983 Cannes Film Festival. Its cultural impact was profound, as President Ronald Reagan, a family friend of the screenwriter, watched the film and ordered a national security review that led to the enactment of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986. The movie also popularized the term "wardialing" (demon dialing) after scenes of a character scanning telephone numbers with a modem.
